It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. \n\nIt actually reminds me a lot of how the administration communicates at the university. I'm a teaching assistant, and they just changed our whole grading portal without telling anyone. Typical, right? I spent three hours yesterday just trying to input midterm scores. The students get so panicked if their grades aren't up immediately. When I was doing my graduate work, we had to wait weeks for a paper to come back, and we survived just fine. Though, to be fair, I did spend most of that time in the library cafe. They had these incredible blueberry scones... I wonder if they still make them. The baker there used real butter, you could always tell. \n\nBut, uh, anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, my wife just thought it would be a good idea for me to come in and talk to someone.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe for certain that your wife’s work messages contain hidden signals meant specifically for you?\n\nPatient: I mean, yes, absolutely. Like I was just saying, if you look at a whole year of these late meetings and the little shifts in how she writes her messages, it’s just too precise to be an accident. I know she claims it's just normal office stuff, but it's clearly a private signal meant for me. She's trying to tell me something without actually saying it out loud. \n\nIt’s a lot like analyzing literature, really. You have to look at the subtext. I try to teach my students about subtext, but getting them to even read the main text is a battle these days. Just last week, I had a sophomore ask if they could listen to a podcast instead of reading the assigned journal article. A podcast! I mean, I do listen to podcasts when I commute—there's a really good one about the history of the Roman Empire, the host does all these different voices for the historical figures—but you can't cite a podcast in a serious research paper. Well, actually, maybe you can with the new APA guidelines. They change the formatting rules every few years anyway. It's completely impossible to keep track of where the commas are supposed to go now. \n\nBut, um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my wife's emails. Yeah, I'm certain there's a hidden message in them.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. It's just the messages, the patterns in the text. I mean, my hearing is perfectly fine. Actually, I think it might be a little too good sometimes. The walls in our apartment building are incredibly thin. The couple next door just got a new puppy, and I swear I can hear every time its little claws click against their hardwood floor. It’s a beagle, I think. They have that very distinct, sort of mournful howl. \n\nMy uncle used to have a beagle when I was growing up. Buster, his name was. He was an absolute menace, always getting into the trash. We had to put these childproof locks on all the lower cabinets just to keep him out of the kitchen. Uncle Frank got so frustrated once that he tried to build this elaborate wooden barricade, but Buster just chewed right through it. Frank was a carpenter, too, so you'd think he would have built something sturdier. He made this beautiful oak dining table for my parents as a wedding gift. It’s still in their dining room, actually, not a single scratch on it after forty years. \n\nWait, what did you ask me? Something about hearing things? No, no voices. Just the regular apartment noise.\n\nDoctor: Do people often tell you that your speech is hard to follow because you go off on tangents?\n\nPatient: Hard to follow? I don't think so. I mean, my wife sometimes sighs and says I'm taking the long way around to a point, but I think that's just because I like to give context. Context is everything, especially in my field. You can't just read a historical document without understanding the political climate of the time. It's like trying to understand the French Revolution without knowing about the bread shortages. \n\nActually, I tried making my own sourdough bread during the pandemic, like everyone else did. I got this starter going—I named him Dough-B-Wan Kenobi, my students thought that was hilarious—and I kept him alive for a solid eight months. But then we had that awful heatwave last summer, and our building's AC went out for three days. It was unbearable. I tried putting the starter in the fridge to slow it down, but I think I shocked it or something. It just never bubbled the same way after that. It's a shame, too, because I was getting really good at scoring the top of the loaves. I bought one of those special little razor blades on a stick... a lame, I think it's called? It's a French word. \n\nAnyway, sorry, you were asking if people say I'm hard to follow? No, not really. I think I communicate pretty clearly, all things considered.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel that your thoughts are being put into your mind by someone else?\n\nPatient: Put into my mind? No, no, they're my thoughts. I mean, nobody's beaming things into my head or anything like that. My thoughts are my own, they just... they just get a little busy sometimes, you know? Like a crowded highway. \n\nSpeaking of highways, the traffic on I-95 this morning was just atrocious. I don't know why they decided to do construction on the southbound lane right during rush hour. It backed up for miles. I was sitting there, listening to the radio, and they were playing this old jazz station. I used to play the saxophone in high school, actually. Alto sax. I wasn't very good, but I loved the shiny brass. My parents rented it for me from this little music shop downtown that smelled like cork grease and old paper. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he had this huge collection of vintage metronomes. Just shelves and shelves of them ticking away. It was almost hypnotic, standing in there. \n\nI tried to find a metronome app for my phone the other day, just to help me pace my grading, but they all have these annoying ads that pop up right when you're trying to focus. It's impossible to concentrate when you're suddenly getting yelled at to buy car insurance. \n\nUm, but what were you asking? Oh, about thoughts being put in my head? No, definitely not. Just my own thoughts in there.\n\nDoctor: Have you tended to avoid other people because you feel uncomfortable or suspicious around them?\n\nPatient: Avoid people? Uncomfortable? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still go to work, I still see my students. I hold office hours every Tuesday and Thursday. It's just that lately, not as many students have been showing up. Which is fine, really, it gives me more time to focus on my own research. \n\nI've been looking into the trade routes of the Hanseatic League in the 14th century. It's fascinating how much power a merchant guild could wield over entire nations. They practically controlled the Baltic Sea. I actually took a trip to Lübeck a few years ago, before the pandemic. Beautiful city. The Holstentor—that big brick gate—it's just stunning in person. They have this incredible marzipan there, too. Niederegger, I think the brand is called. My wife loves marzipan, so I brought back this huge assortment box. It had all these different flavors... pistachio, espresso, orange. We kept it in the pantry, but I think the humidity got to it eventually, because the last few pieces went a bit stale. \n\nIt's funny how humidity affects things. Like the pages of old books, they get all wavy if you don't store them right. The library at the university has this special climate-controlled rare book room. You have to wear these little white cotton gloves if you want to handle anything in there. I always feel like a magician when I put them on. \n\nWait, sorry, what was the question? Something about avoiding people? No, I'm fine around people. Just busy with my work, mostly.\n\nDoctor: Have these beliefs about your wife’s messages caused problems with how you function at work or at home?\n\nPatient: Well, at work, no, not really. My wife and I have had these repeated, really strained conversations about it. It actually got to the point where our couples therapist suggested I come get an individual assessment. \n\nTherapy is strange, isn't it? Sitting on those couches. Ours has this patterned upholstery that looks exactly like the curtains my grandmother had in her living room back in Ohio. She had this huge bay window where she kept African violets. Dozens of them, in these little clay pots. You have to be so careful watering them, you know, because if you get water on the leaves, they rot. You have to water them from the bottom. She had these special little saucers for every single pot. I tried keeping an African violet once in my office, but the fluorescent lights just didn't agree with it. It got all leggy and sad looking. I ended up giving it to the department secretary, Linda. She has a real green thumb. Her desk looks like a jungle. I hate dusting. No, no one's ever said anything like that to me. I've always been pretty normal, I think. Just a regular guy, going about my business, grading papers... 

I grade a lot of papers, actually. Being a teaching assistant for the intro history classes means I'm buried in essays by midterms. The students these days, though, their writing skills are just atrocious. It's like they've never been taught how to construct a proper paragraph, let alone a cohesive argument. They rely so much on spellcheck and grammar apps, but those programs don't catch everything. They certainly don't teach you how to think critically. 

I was reading this article the other day about how handwriting is becoming a lost art. It's really a shame. I always use a fountain pen when I'm grading. A Lamy Safari, charcoal black, with a fine nib. It just glides across the paper. There's something so satisfying about the physical act of writing with a good pen. You have to use the right ink, though. I prefer a deep, rich blue, like a sapphire. The cheap inks tend to feather and bleed through the paper, especially on the thin notebook paper the students use. 

I remember when I was in grade school, we actually had penmanship classes. We had to practice making those perfect cursive loops for hours. My teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was a stickler for neatness. If you smudged your ink, you had to start the whole page over. She had this enormous collection of brooches, a different one for every day of the month, I swear. One was shaped like a little silver owl with green glass eyes. I used to stare at it while she was lecturing about the Civil War. 

But no, to answer your question, nobody has ever told me I act odd or eccentric. I'm just me.

It’s a beagle, I think. They have that very distinct, sort of mournful howl. \n\nMy uncle used to have a beagle when I was growing up. Buster, his name was. Uncle Frank got so frustrated once that he tried to build this elaborate wooden barricade, but Buster just chewed right through it. Frank was a carpenter, too, so you'd think he would have built something sturdier. He made this beautiful oak dining table for my parents as a wedding gift. It’s still in their dining room, actually, not a single scratch on it after forty years. \n\nWait, what did you ask me? Something about hearing things? No, no voices. Just the regular apartment noise.\n\nDoctor: Do people often tell you that your speech is hard to follow because you go off on tangents?\n\nPatient: Hard to follow? I don't think so. I mean, my wife sometimes sighs and says I'm taking the long way around to a point, but I think that's just because I like to give context. Context is everything, especially in my field. You can't just read a historical document without understanding the political climate of the time. No, she hasn't admitted it. She always just says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. But for the past year, they’ve lined up way too precisely to feel accidental, you know? It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly.

He said using a pencil meant you lacked confidence in your answers. 

I tried getting into those cryptic crosswords they have in the British papers, but they're a completely different beast. You really have to think laterally. But anyway, no, she hasn't admitted it. I just know there's something there she isn't telling me.

An affair? No, no, I don't think it's an affair. I don't get the sense that there's another man involved or anything like that. It's more about the messages themselves, the structure of them, you know?
